summary:
HALO (Health Assessment & Longitudinal Observer) is a local on-board health companion for astronauts on long-duration missions. Each day, wearables record vitals, and crew members add their sleep, mood and symptoms. HALO compares every reading to that astronaut’s own pre-flight baseline rather than a population average. It shows five body systems (cardiovascular, immune, musculoskeletal, behavioral and cabin environment) as green, yellow or red, each with a simple reason. An AI assistant explains what changed and what to do. Hard red lines, such as low blood oxygen, high fever or chest pain, always escalate to the ground. We tested HALO on a simulated 180-day mission with four astronauts. It caught all 20 injected health events, on average 3.4 days after they began, with no false alarms.

This matters because beyond low Earth orbit, help is minutes away. Signals from Mars can take up to 22 minutes each way. Many health problems build slowly and hide in day-to-day noise. HALO runs detection on board, so crews can spot trouble early and act without waiting for Earth.
details:
What it does and how it works

HALO (Health Assessment & Longitudinal Observer) is a health companion for astronauts on long missions. It watches each crew member’s daily data and flags problems early.

  1. Daily check-in. Each day HALO records resting heart rate, heart rate variability (HRV), sleep, body temperature, blood oxygen (SpO₂), exercise and time spent with crewmates. Astronauts also report mood, fatigue and symptoms such as headache or back pain, and the cabin’s CO₂ level is logged too.
  2. Personal baseline. HALO learns each astronaut’s own normal from at least 14 pre-flight days. It uses the median and median absolute deviation, so one unusual day doesn’t distort the baseline. A minimum spread per metric keeps ordinary noise from looking like an alarm.
  3. Detection, in three layers:
    • Single readings are scored by how far they fall from baseline, in the direction that matters. For example, heart rate going up or HRV going down.
    • Slow trends are caught with smoothing and drift tracking (EWMA and CUSUM), which find gradual changes like heart-rate drift.
    • Multi-signal rules combine evidence. For example, a fever with a raised heart rate and fatigue points to a possible infection. A CO₂ rise with headaches is treated as a habitat problem for the whole crew.
  4. Red lines. SpO₂ below 92%, a temperature above 39 °C, or chest pain always make the status red and escalate, whatever the rules or the AI say.
  5. Dashboard. Five body systems (cardiovascular, immune, musculoskeletal, behavioral, environment) show as green, yellow or red. Each comes with a plain-language reason.
  6. AI assistant. The planned assistant, built on Gemini, explains what changed and suggests next steps.

Benefits

  • Early warning. On a simulated 180-day mission with four astronauts, HALO caught all 20 injected events, one per body system per astronaut. Fever and CO₂ events were caught the same day, and the mean time to detect was 3.4 days. There were no false alarms across 376 normal astronaut-days.
  • Personalized. It compares each person to their own normal, not to a population average.
  • Works without Earth. Detection runs on board, so it doesn’t depend on a slow or broken link to the ground.
  • Easy to read. Colors always come with words, so astronauts don’t have to interpret raw data.
  • Safe by design. Red lines can’t be overruled by the AI.

Intended impact

On missions to the Moon and Mars, crews will make more medical decisions on their own. HALO aims to give them an always-on health monitor that catches problems while they are still small and easy to manage. It also reduces the workload on the crew and the flight surgeon. The same approach could help people in other remote, isolated settings, such as Antarctic stations, submarines or rural care.

Tools and technologies

Area

Tools

Frontend

React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Lucide icons

Backend

Python, FastAPI

Detection and simulation

pandas, NumPy, YAML config, pytest

AI assistant

Google Gemini (handled by the backend)

Design

Figma, custom mascot and space artwork

Collaboration

Git and GitHub (feature branches, pull requests, shared API contract)

No physical hardware is involved. HALO is designed to take data from space wearables such as the CSA’s Bio-Monitor. For the demo it uses a custom simulator that generates realistic crew data and injects known health events, so detection can be measured.

What makes it creative

  • Tested against known answers. The simulator injects known events, so detection rate, time to detect and false alarms can be measured, not just demonstrated.
  • Detection you can explain. Statistical rules, not a black box, make every flag traceable to specific readings. The AI only explains and advises.
  • The cabin as a patient. Environmental CO₂ is monitored next to human vitals, so a shared cause is flagged across the crew.
  • A friendly face. The HALO robot mascot changes color with health status, which makes the tool approachable on stressful days.

What the team considered

  • Safety: hard red lines, and an AI that can never downgrade a red alert.
  • Communication delay: an offline-first design for deep-space missions.
  • False alarms: tuned to avoid alert fatigue, and measured explicitly.
  • Individual differences: personal baselines with robust statistics.
  • Privacy and security: simulated data only, and API keys kept on the backend.
  • Accessibility: status shown in words as well as color.
  • Honesty: thresholds are marked as prototype values that still need clinical citations and validation.
